items.title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis Garcia Introduction Any team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it. This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out. We believe: A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle. It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations. A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. In our work, an explanation is human-readable evidence for why a title was recommended based on what the member has previously watched, shown on the title’s detail page, which is the screen a member reaches by selecting a title from the homepage. We focus on similarity-based explanations, which connect a recommended title to one reference title the member has interacted with via shared attributes such as genre and tone. For example, A funny, heartfelt holiday romance about love and new beginnings, much like “My Secret Santa.” Quality matters here because a misleading or poorly grounded explanation erodes the very trust the explanation is meant to build. Everything that follows comes out of a series of controlled, user-facing online experiments we ran on the explanation feature, including a month-long experiment on the Netflix mobile app. In these tests we used an LLM to generate explanations, hundreds of thousands a week across a constantly changing catalog. Manually reviewing them at this scale isn’t feasible, so we deployed a second LLM to evaluate them. What counts as a good explanation is specific to our task. However, the way we build, align, and monitor the LLM judge for evaluating explanations should be reusable and generalizable across different tasks. The Lifecycle at a Glance Figure 1 summarizes the four phases of our LLM-judge lifecycle and the data flow connecting them. Figure 1. The four-phase lifecycle of an LLM judge, and the data that flows between the phases. We start with Birth: Benchmark Data Creation, where human experts craft hard or near-boundary examples and human raters label them with pass/fail decisions and written rationales. We augment this with LLM-generated gray-area examples to build a richer benchmark dataset. Next, in the second phase of Training: LLM Judge Development, we tune the LLM judge to align with human labels and rationales from the Birth phase, using self-reflection to identify mismatches between the judge and humans, and updating the rubrics based on those mismatches and anchor examples. We iterate in this phase until our metrics show that the judge is sufficiently aligned with human raters. In the third phase, Deployment, we integrate the judge into the explanation generation system as both a gate and a critic. The LLM generator writes explanations, and the LLM judge scores them and either passes them through or blocks them and supplies a rationale that the generator can use for self-refinement and retries. Passed explanations are served to members, and low-quality explanations are gated. Finally, in the last phase, HITL Alignment & Drift Monitoring, we keep the judge aligned with humans over time. “Human-in-the-loop” here means a person is directly involved in the decision, not just reviewing outcomes after the fact. We benchmark the judge against trained raters, and a human approves every change before it is rolled out to the system. During each test we sampled a set of explanations each week (both passed and gated, with a bias toward newer items), had human raters review them with labels and rationales, and compared the judge against these human ratings. If drift exceeded a threshold, we triggered retraining and benchmark data augmentation. This closes the loop by feeding new human-labeled data and updated signals back into the benchmark and development phases. System components Four automated components appear across all phases, alongside the human roles that define, validate, and supervise them. Generator: produces the explanation text, optionally using prior judge rationales and traces as part of its prompt for revision. Judge: evaluates an explanation and returns a pass/fail label together with a written rationale. In the deployed pipeline, it acts as both a guardrail (gating bad outputs) and a critic (providing feedback for self-refinement). Reflector: revises the Judge’s rubric when the Judge makes mistakes. It updates the rubric based on mismatched examples, human rationales, and anchor examples. It tunes the rubric and does not directly evaluate explanations. Meta-Judge: checks whether the Judge failed an explanation for the right reason by comparing the Judge’s rationale against a human rater’s rationale. Human experts and raters: the experts who define the quality criteria; the raters whose labels and written rationales the Judge is tuned and measured against; the reviewers who monitor the Judge while it is running and explicitly approve any changes before they were rolled out. Phase I, Birth: Establishing Ground Truth Everything downstream depends on knowing what “good” means, so this is the most human-intensive phase. Our internal writing experts define the must-have criteria an explanation must satisfy, author detailed labeling guidelines, and hand-craft tricky adversarial examples. Those same guidelines do double duty. They’re both the rulebook for human raters and the seed rubric for the LLM judges we tune later. Why we built our own benchmark Off-the-shelf LLM-judge benchmarks focus on general-purpose text evaluation and miss what makes our task specific. Explanations are short, item-specific, and context-dependent (each one is tied to a target title and one or two reference titles the member has watched). We also care about alignment to our own editorial bar, not just generic language quality. As a result, we built our own custom benchmark from three complementary sources: Expert-crafted adversarial cases: hand-authored pass/fail examples with known failure modes, the kind of edge cases nothing else reliably produces. Boundary examples: LLM-synthesized explanations that are deliberately pushed near the pass/fail boundary, then rated by humans. These capture the ambiguous cases that sampling from live traffic rarely surfaces on its own. Real sampled explanations: explanations sampled from the output of our LLM generator during test runs. Two details that mattered The benchmark is not frozen. A monitoring pipeline (Phase IV) appends a fresh batch of human-rated explanations on a weekly cadence, so over the course of a test the benchmark tracked the current catalog and new usage patterns instead of going stale. Every “fail” label carries a free-text rationale explaining why the explanation failed. This looks like a small bookkeeping detail, but it is actually critical for the next phase, since those rationales are what we use to tune and audit the judge’s reasoning. Phase II, Training: Aligning the Judge to Humans The failure mode: right answer, wrong reason There is a failure mode that does not show up in label-agreement metrics at all. A judge can agree with humans on the label, passing when they would pass and failing when they would fail, while reaching the right verdict for the wrong reason. On a dashboard it looks perfectly aligned. But as soon as you ask it to explain a rejection, which our pipeline does to steer self-revision, it can return misleading guidance. We therefore care about not just label agreement but also reasoning alignment. In our setup, the Judge is always asked to output: a label (e.g., PASS/FAIL), and a short natural-language rationale for that label. Here is an illustrative example. The member watched a musical, a family fantasy with a young heroine and a well-known ensemble cast. We recommend an adventure movie that is also a family fantasy with a young heroine, which is why the recommender paired them. But it shares neither the songs nor the ensemble cast. The label (FAIL) is correct, and the stated reason is reasonable at first glance. But it turns out to be incomplete in a way that simple label agreement cannot detect, as we show below. Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning We tune each criterion’s LLM Judge with a procedure we call Reasoning-Aligned Rubric Tuning (RART). As introduced in the system components above, the Judge, Meta-Judge, and Reflector are distinct components. The Judge scores an explanation against a rubric and gives a rationale, the Meta-Judge compares that rationale against a human-written one, and the Reflector edits the rubric text itself. RART is how the three are combined into a training loop. Every Judge is a fixed prompt template parameterized by a rubric, so tuning it does not mean retraining the underlying model. Instead we iteratively refine the rubric text until the Judge’s behavior matches human labels and human rationales. At iteration i, the Judge is conditioned on the current rubric text and maps an explanation to a pair, a label and a rationale. R_i is the current rubric text, y_J(x) the label, and r_J(x) the rationale. At a high level, each RART iteration proceeds as follows. Score the training data with the current rubric. Evaluate weighted alignment metrics on a held-out validation set. If all per-criterion metrics exceed their thresholds, stop. Otherwise, construct an error-driven focus set of misaligned examples and hand it to the Reflector, which proposes a revised rubric. The key difference from a standard loop is how we define a “mistake.” Most self-improvement loops look only at label disagreements. RART adds a second class of error. The Meta-Judge examines the cases where the Judge and a human both said fail and compares the Judge’s stated reason against the human’s rationale. When the two diverge, that is a right answer, wrong reason error, and it is also fed to the Reflector. Concretely, the focus set handed to the Reflector is the union of two error classes: Label mismatches: examples where the Judge’s label differs from the human’s. Right label, wrong reason: examples where the Judge and the human both said FAIL, but the Meta-Judge finds their two rationales don’t match. So the Reflector revises the rubric from both ordinary label errors and right label, wrong reason errors. That second term is the core of RART. The Judge is pushed not only to match human decisions but to justify them in a way the Meta-Judge recognizes as aligned with human reasoning. Returning to the earlier example, the LLM Judge said FAIL and a human said FAIL, so a label-only check would register agreement. Placing the two reasons side by side shows what that check misses. RART routes it into the focus set, so the next rubric revision has to account for it. Since the Meta-Judge is an LLM too, we checked it against humans first. Trained human raters labeled a sample of agreed-fail rationale pairs, and the Meta-Judge matched their verdicts on nearly all of them. Alignment metrics We run one Judge per criterion, each with its own rubric, tuned and scored on its own. So everything below is measured per criterion on held-out data. For each one we track three metrics. Specificity (fail-recall): how often the Judge correctly rejects bad explanations. This is the one we care about most, because a bad explanation that slips through the gate is a trust hazard. Recall (pass-recall): how often it correctly passes good explanations, which keeps coverage high and revision cost low. Reasoning agreement: on the explanations both reject, how often they reject for the same reason. Each criterion’s Judge gets its own three, and one can be healthy while another slips. That is also why the gate is strict. An explanation has to pass every must-have criterion to be eligible to serve. Ablation: does the reasoning signal help? To isolate the impact of the reasoning signal, we compare RART to an otherwise identical loop that uses only label disagreements. We call this baseline vanilla: same Reflector, same Judge, same data, but no Meta-Judge and no use of human rationales. Figure 2. Improvement over the starting rubric, per criterion, for reasoning-aware tuning (RART) and label-only tuning (vanilla). Figure 2 shows the result. On two of the three must-have criteria, vanilla and RART land in the same place, because the starting rubric was already near ceiling and the metrics had very little room to gain. On the third criterion, the vanilla (label-only) method degrades. The Reflector in the vanilla loop rewrites the rubric into degenerate forms, and specificity and reasoning agreement fall with every iteration, ending up worse than the rubric it started from. RART stays stable on that same criterion and lifts both, with a small recall gain as well. The reason is that a vanilla (label-only) optimizer can reach the right label through unsound reasoning, and unsound reasoning doesn’t generalize to new data. Anchoring the signal on the rationale prevents that. Reasoning alignment helps where there is headroom and doesn’t hurt where there isn’t. Phase III, Deployment: Putting the Judge to Work Once deployed, the judge sat inside the generation pipeline, gating and critiquing explanations as they were produced during our tests. Two roles for one judge Once we align the LLM Judge with humans, we reuse it in two distinct roles for every generated explanation: Role 1, the gate. The Judge scores each explanation against the must-have criteria and rejects anything that fails. Role 2, the critic. When an explanation fails, we don’t just throw it away. The Judge’s free-text reason gets appended to the Generator’s prompt, and the Generator tries again. The second role turns the pipeline into a generate → judge → revise loop, with the Judge’s critique steering each revision. Bounded retries, and why we drop rather than serve We cap the retries. Each revision costs another round of generation and judging, and the gains flatten quickly. Figure 3 shows what the loop actually buys, on 1,000 generated explanations run through as many as 12 revisions with four generators. Every curve climbs, which is the Judge’s critique doing its job, but the steep part is early, and the gap between generators is obvious. Revision amplifies a capable generator rather than rescuing a weak one. In our test runs we used a budget of 3 retries with our strongest generator, and an explanation still failing after that was dropped rather than served. Figure 3. Cumulative share of explanations that clear the Judge as we allow more revisions, across four generator models. That “drop rather than serve” rule is deliberate. The two outcomes aren’t symmetric. A bad explanation is a trust hazard, while a missing explanation just forgoes an opportunity. When in doubt we’d rather show nothing, and most explanations cleared the bar within the retry budget. Do judge-approved explanations help members? Passing the Judge proves an explanation is good by our standards, but it doesn’t prove that judge-approved explanations are useful to members. To test that connection, we ran a one-time controlled experiment on the Netflix mobile app, explanations vs. no explanations on the title detail page, over roughly a month, with the pipeline generating and judging hundreds of thousands of explanations a week during the period. Members who saw explanations shifted their viewing toward titles they hadn’t watched before, and more of their browse sessions ended in a meaningful play. Both effects were statistically significant, and we saw no member-initiated takedowns or escalations about explanation quality during the test. The result worth carrying over isn’t the size of that effect. It’s that offline agreement with our raters was necessary for these explanations to work but never sufficient to show they help members. Only the online A/B test could establish that judge-aligned explanations are not just quality-compliant but genuinely useful. Phase IV, Monitoring: Keeping the Judge Aligned A judge that’s well aligned at launch won’t stay that way. The catalog shifts, and so does what counts as high quality. The lifecycle has to close the loop. The weekly human review For each week a test was running, we pulled roughly 300 generated explanations for human review, stratified across the Judge’s decisions (served, revised, dropped) and weighted toward newer catalog items, where drift is most likely. The stratification stayed fixed week to week, so successive weeks were comparable. A panel of at least three raters reviewed each explanation, and the majority label was our ground truth. Those labels did two jobs. They told us whether judge-human agreement was slipping, and they grew the benchmark. Setting the bar with human disagreement The panel also tells us how much the raters disagreed with each other, which turns out to be the right yardstick for the Judge. Rather than hold it to a fixed threshold, we score the Judge and each rater against the same majority label and ask that the Judge fall within the raters’ own spread. Take one criterion and one of its metrics, M. That week’s sample gives one value M(J) for the Judge and a set of per-rater values M(H) for the three or more raters on the panel. We require so the Judge must score no worse than two standard deviations below the average rater. A harder week widens human disagreement and widens the band with it, so the Judge isn’t penalized for difficulty the humans also felt. Falling below the band on any metric-criterion pair is a drift event, which triggers re-tuning (back to Phase II) on the augmented benchmark. A re-tuned rubric never goes live automatically. Someone on the team reads the proposed changes and signs off before it reaches the running pipeline, and we keep the previous rubric for instant rollback. What human review catches that metrics can’t Beyond asking whether the Judge still agrees with human raters, the weekly review answers a second question. Are the current guidelines still asking for the right things? In the weekly review process, reviewers surfaced issues that did not show up in Judge–rater agreement. An explanation can use accurate attributes and still overstate how similar two titles really are. A single vague adjective (“exciting”, “fun”, “emotional”) can technically satisfy the rubric while saying almost nothing. Sometimes the reference itself is the problem, something the member wouldn’t think of as a comparable title at all, so the comparison lands oddly no matter how the attributes line up. Some genres show the same problem at scale. Stand-up specials can share similar metadata tags but differ completely in tone and cultural context, so a comparison may look justified on paper, not be bad enough for a rater to fail, and still land poorly with members. And some explanations meet every must-have criterion while still reading like generic “word soup” that does not help the user much. When recurring patterns kept appearing, we updated the Phase I guidelines, which seed both the raters’ instructions and the judges’ rubrics, so one revision updates both sides. Other times we added product rules outside the Judge, for example by blocking certain title types from being used as references. Drift detection catches a judge that has stopped agreeing with people. Only the continued human review tells us when our definition of a “good explanation” is too narrow or incomplete. We need both. Drift detection keeps the Judge aligned with the current rubric. Continuous human review keeps the rubric aligned with what actually works for members. What We Learned Five lessons we think transfer to any team shipping an LLM judge: Invest in the benchmark before the judge. A modest, rationale-annotated benchmark beats a large label-only one. Those written rationales are exactly what make reasoning-aligned tuning possible. You can’t correct a judge’s reasoning if you never wrote down the human’s. Tune on reasoning, not just labels. A judge can reach the right verdict for the wrong reason, which looks fine on a dashboard but gives misleading feedback and doesn’t hold up on new data. In our ablation, the label-only loop degraded a rubric that the reasoning-aware loop kept stable. One aligned judge can serve many roles. Reusing the same judge as both gate and critic amortizes the alignment cost and keeps production behavior consistent across roles. Alignment is the expensive part, so get one judge right and use it more than once. Plan for monitoring from day one. A recommender platform’s items and members never stop changing, so an LLM judge, like any ML model, has to be watched and re-tuned if needed, not shipped and forgotten. Keep people in the loop by design, not by exception. Automating evaluation is not the same as delegating responsibility for it. In our lifecycle, humans set the standard (Phase I), supply the rationales the judge is aligned to (Phase II), decide the conservative default of dropping rather than serving a doubtful output (Phase III), and review a standing sample of live decisions and approve every rubric change before it ships (Phase IV). These checkpoints are much harder to retrofit once a judge is already making decisions on its own. The standing review also tells us what our rubric is missing, not just when our judge has slipped. Taken together, the judge extends the reach of our reviewers, and those reviewers are the basis for trusting the judge. That relationship is what makes it responsible to run this system at scale. An automated evaluator that no one audits provides no assurance about the decisions it is making. Acknowledgements This post summarizes our research paper, “The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge for Large-Scale Recommendation Explanations,” which has the full methodology, metrics, and ablations. Our thanks to the internal human writers and review experts who defined what a good explanation is and keep those guidelines current; to our Human Data Operations team and the raters they train and calibrate, whose labels and written rationales are what the judges are aligned to; and to the engineers across the team who built and operate the pipeline; and to our UI engineering partners, who built the member-facing surfaces that bring these explanations to the homepage. The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile. A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result. That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way. The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks. While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely. To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it. The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow, Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development: our workflows run on Maestro (Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment, then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs. With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment. I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job. Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required. The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging. The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other. While the previous chart shows the time savings, the architecture that enables this isolation looks like below: How an AI Agent Helped Running five parallel experiments gets messy fast. Tracking instance IDs, configs, memory spills, and stage failures across variants makes it easy to lose track. This is where an AI agent stepped in, not to write clever code, but to handle operational grunt work. I described variants in plain English, and the agent updated scheduler configs, deployed to the branch, triggered jobs, and polled metrics. Once complete, it compared spill and failure counts across variants in a summary table, allowing me to ask, “Which run is closest to OOM-free at peak load?” and get an immediate answer. The value wasn’t deep Spark expertise, but operational memory. It turned tedious Spark UI cross-checks into a single prompt. Eventually, I packaged this workflow into a reusable agent skill (.agents/skills/sandbox-deploy-and-run/) run via /sandbox-deploy-and-run <module> <scheduler-file> [PARAM=value]. It handles the full lifecycle—preflight, deploy, background polling, auto-diagnostics, and re-entrant resume <instance_id> support—turning multi-hour experiments into a single command. Why tmux Mattered All of this ran on Workbench, Netflix’s cloud dev environment, using my laptop as a thin terminal. Without session persistence, an SSH drop or sleeping laptop would kill multi-hour Spark runs mid-flight. tmux running directly on Workbench solved this. Every experiment lived in a named cloud session: I could close my laptop, reattach hours later, and pick up where I left off. Combined with branch isolation, this made "start five and walk away" possible. This is now my default setup: a local terminal (Ghostty), dedicated git worktrees per branch, and persistent tmux sessions on Workbench. The local laptop is disposable—closing it or losing network never interrupts the jobs. That setup turned a long travel day into active iteration time. I kicked off batches at the gate, checked results via AI agent over spotty inflight Wi-Fi, and squeezed 4–5 full experiment cycles into a single 24-hour flight. What All Experiments Uncovered The root cause came down to a single operator: collect_list. Because Spark buffers each full event bag in memory, long-session OOMs were driven by individual bag size, not total dataset volume. The legacy pipeline handled identical row counts without crashing, proving that each event in the new bag had grown significantly heavier. Two factors inflated event weight: Field types and Option boxing: The session ID changed from an 8-byte Long to a UUID string. Worse, wrapping fields in Scala Option forced Spark to deserialize typed Datasets into JVM objects (Some wrappers), driving up object allocation and GC pressure across tens of thousands of events per session. Bloated string attributes: Low-value fields (e.g., referrer URLs, test allocations) added several hundred bytes per event. Multiplying these strings across collect_list wasted terabytes per hour, even though downstream tasks rarely used them. The Fixes: Unboxed primitives: Removing Option wrappers from non-nullable fields dropped peak executor memory from 112% to 58% of the slot with zero disk spill. Slimmed event bags: Dropped unused per-event attributes and hoisted session-invariant metadata (app version, country) up to the session header. Takeaway: Reducing individual event weight delivered far better stability than throwing more cluster memory at the problem. Two Experiments That Changed My Mind Out of dozens of runs, two findings completely overturned my assumptions about Spark memory management: Finding 1: Narrowing rows can trigger faster OOMs. Slimming our table dropped its size below Spark’s auto-broadcast threshold, prompting the query planner to switch from shuffle joins to broadcast joins. Because broadcast joins pin build-side tables directly into executor memory, narrower rows actually increased total memory pressure. Finding 2: Broadcast hash joins were silently draining memory. Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) rewrote nine sort-merge joins into broadcast hash joins at runtime. While each join stayed under our 400 MB broadcast limit individually, AQE pinned ~3.1 GB of cumulative data simultaneously in a single executor, pushing containers over the edge. The Surgical Fix: Instead of disabling broadcast joins globally, I lowered only AQE’s runtime threshold (spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold) to 10 MB while leaving the compile-time threshold untouched. That single change freed up ~3.1 GB of executor memory without impacting initial query planning. Takeaway: Broadcast joins speed up queries, but pinned memory isn’t free. Watch accumulated broadcasts in your execution plan, not just dataset sizes. Keeping a Single Experiment Log When running dozens of parallel tests, the biggest risk isn’t job failure, it’s losing track of what you’ve already tried or confusing which JAR and config produced a result. To solve this, I scaffolded the AI agent to append a row to a repository Markdown table after every run: Run # | Jar ver | Change vs. Previous Run | Config | Key Metrics (Spill, Failed Tasks, Peak Memory, Duration) If a run yielded a key finding, the agent added a short note explaining what the result proved or disproved. Key Takeaways: Single source of truth: It created an auditable history for the entire investigation. Forced discipline: Requiring “Change vs. Previous Run” forced me to isolate variables. Whenever I bundled multiple changes, I couldn’t isolate the root cause and had to rerun the test — a mistake the log format immediately exposed. A secondary doc (events-join-spark-tuning.md) captured the distilled findings as a quick "symptom-to-knob" lookup, so teammates didn't have to wade through the full chronological history. A Mistake I Learned From: The Fix That Only Worked Off-Peak. To cap session size, I added row_number().over(Window...) and filtered for the first N events. It passed off-peak tests cleanly, but crashed with OOMs at peak load. The issue was structural: Spark’s Window operator buffers an entire session in memory before evaluating row numbers and filtering. The cap trimmed output downstream, but it didn't limit memory usage during buffering, so a single skewed session overwhelmed executor memory. The Fix & Lesson: We moved truncation ahead of the Window stage to cap events before buffering occurs. Takeaway: Test fixes against worst-case input skew. Off-peak runs hide structural bottlenecks that peak scale will immediately trigger. The final fix Pulling it together, four changes shipped, each isolated to a single experiment before it landed: Unboxed the never-null fields from Option to plain primitives. Peak executor memory dropped from about 112% of the slot to about 58%, with zero spill. Slimmed the event bag. Dropped per-event fields nobody used, and hoisted session-invariant fields (versions, country, connection type) to the session level so they are stored once per session, not once per event. Capped session size before the Window stage. Dropped oversized sessions ahead of the buffering, and truncated the bag to the cap rather than dropping whole sessions. Lowered AQE’s runtime broadcast threshold. Set spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to 10 MB, leaving the compile-time threshold untouched. The Unresolved Bottleneck While these fixes made the pipeline run cleanly, they didn’t solve the underlying scaling issue: aggregating an entire session’s event bag into a single row has a hard ceiling. As our upstream telemetry source evolves and adds new attributes, each event in the bag becomes heavier, meaning this memory pressure will eventually return without a single line of code changing on our end. Slimming and unboxing bought us headroom, but they didn’t change the fundamental data shape. The biggest takeaway from this effort is that tuning buys time, not infinite scale. If your underlying data model allows unbounded row growth, tuning alone won’t save you , eventually, the architecture itself has to change. Summary If the bug only appears at scale, stop trying to sample. Build a way to run many full-scale runs in parallel instead. If your scheduler can use the branch name, then one branch becomes one isolated experiment, and running many at once becomes easy. Use an AI agent to run the operation, not only to write code. Deploy, poll, pull metrics, compare variants: this is where most of the time goes. Once a loop repeats, package it as a skill. The deploy-run-watch-diagnose cycle becomes one command. Use tmux for long runs. The run must survive you closing the laptop. Keep one single experiment log, and make every entry state the one change from the previous run. The format itself forces you to change one variable at a time. For memory problems, look at the per-row width first, not only at the total data volume. Bigger field types, Option boxing, and fat unused strings all add up inside a collect_list bag. Tuning buys headroom, not a new ceiling. If the data shape can grow without a bound, the design has to change eventually, tuning alone will not save you. items.title: Netflix Conductor: The Next Chapter
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: Netflix Conductor : The Next Chapter by Aravindan Ramkumar on behalf of the Conductor team Conductor is the workflow orchestration engine Netflix uses to stitch micro-services into reliable, observable business processes. If you’ve followed Conductor from the outside, the last thing you heard was probably the note on its GitHub repository: Netflix discontinued maintenance of Conductor OSS to refocus its resources on the internal fork. That announcement marked the end of the open-source chapter, and from the outside it may have looked like the end of the story. It wasn’t. Internally, Conductor never slowed down. If anything, it grew faster, and the demands of that growth pushed us to rebuild it from the ground up. This post is the answer to the natural question that announcement leaves open: what happened to Conductor after that? A lot, it turns out. The clearest way to put it is in terms of growth. Not long ago, Conductor crossing a billion workflow executions in a single year felt like a milestone. Today it clears that bar roughly every quarter, and the monthly volume is still climbing. Sustaining that kind of growth meant rethinking nearly every layer of the system. The data plane it runs on was modernized piece by piece. The evaluation engine was rewritten. The way it allocates work, controls concurrency, and runs compute all changes. The through-line is simple: scale forced a rethink of the evaluation engine and the layers beneath it, and everything else followed. The rest of this post walks through that evolution: how the architecture changed, the performance and scale work at the heart of it, the leap forward in developer experience, and the newer capabilities for controlling how workflows and tasks execute. How Netflix uses Conductor When we last wrote about Conductor, it ran a few hundred workflow definitions for a few dozen teams. That footprint has grown by orders of magnitude. Conductor now backs roughly 200,000 workflow definitions owned by around 150 applications, spanning Content and Studio Engineering, Ads, Games, and more. The runtime side has grown to match. In a typical month it executes on the order of 420 million workflows, and on a given day it runs anywhere from 5 to 20 million, with teams adding hundreds of new workflow types every month. Conductor and the Media Production Suite One of the clearest ways to see what Conductor does is Netflix’s Media Production Suite (MPS). It’s a set of applications that move production data into the cloud. An average Netflix title generates around 200 terabytes of original camera files, and MPS is what gets that media ingested, validated, transcoded, and delivered to the right people around the world. The multi-step pipelines behind MPS’s workflows (Footage Ingest, Dailies, VFX Pulls, and Conform Pulls) run as Conductor workflows. A dedicated orchestration layer called Studio Orchestrator stitches together the platform services these pipelines depend on, such as asset management, media encoding, and storage, using Conductor under the hood to ensure reliable execution and the durability to recover from the inevitable failures of long-running, distributed work. Beyond the studio: Ads and Games Content engineering is where Conductor started, but it’s no longer the whole story. Two of Netflix’s newer businesses lean on it just as heavily. Netflix Ads has made Conductor a backbone of its programmatic pipelines. Creative ingestion, advertiser-certificate management, and privacy-preserving Data Clean Rooms all run as Conductor workflows. Netflix Games uses Conductor to orchestrate the path a game takes from a partner’s submission to the app stores. When a studio uploads a build, a Conductor pipeline ingests the binary, runs the required validations (for example, iOS privacy-manifest checks), and drives App Store publishing, coordinating steps that span multiple platform services and external stores with the same reliability and visibility the studio pipelines rely on. How the architecture evolved Our earlier post described a Conductor built on a particular set of building blocks: DynoQueues for queueing, Dynomite for metadata, Cassandra (partially) for execution data, and Elasticsearch for indexing. That stack carried Conductor a long way, but as adoption climbed, almost every layer of it was eventually rethought. The data plane Conductor runs on today looks very little like the earlier one. 1.0: the original stack, and where it strained In its first generation, Conductor leaned heavily on Dynomite (with DynoQueues as the queueing recipe layered on top) backed by Elasticsearch for indexing. It worked, but two classes of problems showed up as scale grew. The first was the datastore. Dynomite is an in-memory store: a clustering layer that adds sharding and replication on top of Redis. You scale it by adding memory and nodes, with each replica rack holding a full copy of the data, which suits a cache but not the durable record for millions of workflows a day. Dyno Queues, built on the same store, inherited those limits, and its zone-sharded design made task scheduling uneven. The second was the engine’s design: evaluation ran synchronously and mutated workflow state in several places, so competing updates could leave a workflow inconsistent with no automated way to repair it. The 2.x line was a sustained campaign to address these, and two replacements did most of the heavy lifting. 2.0: Cassandra as the backbone The most consequential change was making Cassandra the primary datastore for execution data, displacing Dynomite. Cassandra gave Conductor the elastic, horizontal scaling it needed, and removed the scaling ceiling and zone-affinity constraints that the old datastore imposed. Around the same time, large task inputs and outputs were offloaded to S3, keeping bulky data off the primary datastore and further easing the pressure on it. Timestone: a purpose-built queueing layer The second replacement was the queue itself. Timestone, Netflix’s high-throughput, low-latency priority queueing system, took over from DynoQueues. Beyond shedding the Dynomite dependency, it brought two capabilities that mattered for reliability: a delayed-queuing mechanism, and a background repair process that could detect and recover workflows. Timestone also turned out to be foundational for work that came later. The async evaluation queue and the queue-depth-driven dynamic thread allocation described later in this post both build on it. Alongside these, the 2.x series also decoupled indexing from the critical path, moving to a Kafka-buffered, independently scalable indexer writing to Elasticsearch. 3.0: consolidating the modern data plane By Conductor 3.0, these threads came together into a coherent platform. Dynomite was fully sunset. Timestone was the queue and Cassandra the datastore. A Kafka-fed indexer pushed to Elasticsearch, with Iceberg added for long-term storage. The release also shipped automated workflow repair and multi-cluster deployment, the last of which lets workflows run in fully isolated contexts (for example, a dedicated context for the Media Production Suite, kept separate from the shared default and scaled on its own). The net effect is that by 3.0 the foundational reliability and scaling problems of the early era were largely solved, and the data plane reached roughly the shape it has today. 1.0 to 3.0 architecture evolution Rebuilding the engine: Conductor 4.0 By 3.0, everything around the evaluation engine had been modernized, but the engine and its data model were largely the original, and at this scale that became the bottleneck. The engine evaluated a workflow by loading its entire state into memory to decide what to do next, which meant heavy memory pressure and slow evaluations as workflows grew toward tens of thousands of tasks. It also stored a workflow’s metadata and its task payloads in the same Cassandra partition, producing oversized “wide rows” and leaving room for race conditions when several updates to the same task competed. Evaluation overhead, vertical-scaling pressure, and occasional inconsistent state needed to be addressed. A partitioned task model The old data model co-located everything about a workflow in one place. The rewrite separates workflow metadata from task and user data and gives each task its own record. The engine no longer loads the whole workflow graph to make a decision. It evaluates against a lightweight blueprint of the workflow and loads only the specific task data a decision needs. The practical result is a dramatically smaller memory footprint per evaluation and far less work to advance a workflow by one step. The 3.0 engine topped out around 2,500 tasks per workflow. The rewritten engine scales to 30,000 tasks per workflow, more than a 10x increase. Evaluation got faster too: in production, the rewrite delivered roughly a 40% reduction in p99 workflow-evaluation latency. Metric graph showing a reduction in workflow-evaluation latency Making competing updates safe using partitions Separating the data is only half the story. The engine also has to make competing updates to the same task safe, because a task can be written from more than one place at once. Picture a long-running task whose worker sends periodic updates to keep it alive, each one marking the task in-progress, before finally reporting it COMPLETED. If a stray in-progress update arrives just after that completion, reordered by the network, it could quietly revert a COMPLETED task back to IN_PROGRESS. The first version leaned on Cassandra lightweight transactions (LWT) to serialize these writes, but mixing LWT with ordinary writes is a known Cassandra anti-pattern. The two use different timestamping mechanisms, and combining them breaks the strict consistency Conductor needs. So the data model evolved away from locking entirely. Task state is split across two partitions: a pending partition for tasks still in flight, and a terminal partition that a task is written to exactly once, when it reaches a terminal state (COMPLETED, FAILED, etc). When the engine evaluates a workflow, it reads both and reconciles them in the application layer with one simple rule: a terminal state always wins over a non-terminal one, and between two writes of the same kind (two in-progress, or two terminal) ordinary last-write-wins applies. So in the race above, when the task is marked COMPLETED it lands in the terminal partition, and the late in-progress update loses on read. Race condition illustration The net of the rewrite is reliable task lifecycle management, a lower memory footprint, faster evaluation, and far higher concurrent throughput. Conductor 4.0 — Architecture Removing the last synchronous bottleneck: async workflow evaluation A faster engine still left one structural problem. Workflow evaluation ran synchronously. When an update arrived, a new workflow or a task completing, the request itself evaluated the workflow, and to do that safely it had to take a lock on that workflow. Under load, concurrent updates to the same workflow raced for that lock. Only one won, and the rest were deferred to a background repair process that, in extreme cases, could take several minutes to catch up. The result was exactly the kind of unpredictable tail latency that hurts most under peak load. The fix was to decouple the trigger from the evaluation. Updates no longer evaluate inline. Instead they enqueue the workflow onto a Timestone exclusive queue, and a central asynchronous evaluator processes each workflow’s pending work in order. Because the queue is exclusive, only one worker ever evaluates a given workflow at a time, so the lock contention simply goes away. The results are most dramatic at the tail (p99 and p99.9), which is the point, since the tail is what users feel under load: Unsuccessful lock-acquire attempts, which had spiked to around 2,700 per interval under contention, drop to essentially zero with async evaluation. Unsuccessful lock acquistion attempts reducing to zero Controlling how workflows execute Run Strategies: native control over workflow concurrency For most of its life, Conductor would happily run as many instances of a workflow as you started, all at once. That’s the right default, but it left a gap. When several workflow instances act on the same entity, the same movie id, the same creative, the same script, there is no built-in way to serialize them or guarantee only one runs at a time. Teams that needed this had to build it themselves: custom locks, custom queues, custom coordination logic bolted onto their workflows. That’s extra complexity in every workflow that needs it, and a real source of operational risk. Run Strategies are a way to declare, on a workflow definition, how concurrent executions should be handled. There are two strategies today. Parallel, the default, applies no restrictions and behaves exactly as workflows always have. Sequential runs at most one workflow at a time per sequence key, with subsequent requests enqueued and started automatically, in order, as each running workflow finishes. A run strategy is declared on the workflow definition, and can be set directly in the Workflow SDK as a @RunStrategy annotation argument on the @WorkflowMethod. The key idea is the sequence key: two executions that share a sequence key run one after another, and executions with different keys still run in parallel. So a content-ingestion workflow keyed on movie id processes each title strictly serially while happily running many different titles concurrently, with no custom locking required. Beyond polled workers: managed, serverless tasks A task meant a polled worker: your application implements the worker, polls the Conductor server for work, runs it, and reports the result back. That model is simple and language-agnostic, and it’s still the backbone for most workloads. But it has a cost. You operate the worker fleet. You stand it up, keep it running, and scale it, even for work that’s bursty or runs rarely. So Conductor added managed tasks: built-in task types where Conductor drives the compute directly, with no long-lived worker for you to host or scale. Two integrations carry most of this today: Titus for containers and Stratum for serverless media-processing functions. A TITUS task launches a Titus job to run a script, whether shell, Python, or whatever your image packages, using Titus, Netflix’s container management platform, as the compute plane. You point the task at a Docker image and an entry point, and specify the shape of the run, such as cpu and memory. The lifecycle is fully managed. The task starts IN_PROGRESS, Conductor monitors the Titus job, and it transitions on the container’s exit behavior. An exit code of 0 marks the task COMPLETED, and a non-zero code, a timeout, or a missing job marks it FAILED. The upshot is that you can spin up containerized compute as a step in a workflow without running a worker that sits around polling. A STRATUM task invokes a Stratum function and collects its output. Stratum is the serverless function layer of Netflix’s Cosmos platform, purpose-built for media-processing workloads, and a Conductor STRATUM task is the natural way to call one from a workflow. You give it a function name and an ordered list of arguments. The task stays IN_PROGRESS until the function finishes, then resolves to COMPLETED, FAILED, or TIMED_OUT. Because Stratum exposes functions to Conductor directly, teams can fold resource-intensive media operations into a workflow without owning the compute that runs them. Polled workers, Titus jobs, and Stratum functions are three points on a spectrum, and a single workflow can mix all three: a long-lived worker for steady high-volume work, a Titus container for an occasional heavy batch step, and a Stratum function for media processing. Managed tasks shift the operational burden from the team to the platform. Scaling task polling: dynamic thread allocation The engine work in the previous section made Conductor evaluate workflows fast. But there’s a second half to throughput: how quickly workers pick up the tasks that evaluation schedules. That’s a polling problem, and at scale it has its own failure mode, one that showed up most sharply for Studio Orchestrator, the heavy Conductor user behind the Media Production Suite pipelines from earlier in this post. Conductor clients poll for work using worker threads, and historically the number of threads was fixed per task type. That’s predictable, and it prevents any one task from starving the others, but it’s static. During burst traffic, when thousands of instances of a single task suddenly pile into a queue, a fixed thread count can’t ramp up to drain them. The symptom was distinctive: CPU on the instances stayed flat while queues backed up, and idle threads sat stranded on quiet queues unable to help the overloaded one. Allocating threads by real-time queue depth The fix is a dynamic allocation strategy that rebalances threads across task queues continuously, based on how much work each queue actually has, while still guaranteeing every queue a floor so nothing starves. Each instance periodically polls Timestone for the current depth of every task queue it manages. It then splits its thread pool into two parts. A minimum allocation gives every queue a baseline number of threads, so no queue is ever fully starved. A floating pool holds the remaining threads, distributed across queues in proportion to each queue’s share of the total load. A queue with a deep backlog draws a large slice of the floating pool. An idle queue falls back toward its minimum, freeing threads for whoever needs them. One guardrail keeps this from becoming its own problem: a multiplier ceiling. A queue’s thread count can grow by at most a configurable factor per cycle, so even a dramatic load spike ramps up in controlled steps rather than all at once, giving downstream and dependent services time to absorb the increase instead of being bombarded. Allocations are recomputed every polling interval, so the system tracks shifting load in near real time while always honoring the per-queue minimums. Two things come out of this. First, because threads are allocated where they’re actually needed, each instance can safely run a much larger pool. Second, CPU utilization becomes an accurate signal of how busy an instance is, which means autoscaling on CPU makes the cluster scale out in response to real computational demand. Developer experience: Workflow SDK For most of Conductor’s life, authoring a workflow meant writing JSON. You declared each task, then wired one task’s output into the next with ${taskRef.output.field} string templates, and on the worker side you pulled inputs back out of a Map<String, Object> and cast them to the types you expected. It worked, but it pushed an entire class of errors to runtime, and made large workflows genuinely hard to read. The Workflow SDK is our answer: a type-safe Java DSL for authoring Conductor workflows. You write Java code. The compiler and IDE catch mistakes before anything deploys, and a Gradle plugin translates your Java code into the JSON workflow definition the Conductor server understands. Crucially, the SDK gives you the best of both worlds. One of Conductor’s defining strengths has always been visibility. Because a workflow is a declared graph rather than imperative code, during execution the exact control flow can be inspected, every branch, loop, and parallel fork, and light up live as an execution moves through it. Writing workflows in imperative code gives you none of that. A timeline is not a workflow diagram. The SDK keeps both halves. You write in idiomatic Java and at execution time you still get the full visual graph: the same task-by-task flow, inputs and outputs, and at-a-glance “where is this stuck and why” that Conductor has always offered. The authoring pains it removes No type safety. In the JSON model, a task input like “movieId”: “${awesomeTask2.output.movieId}” is just a string template. The worker reads it back with inputData.get(“movieId”) and casts. If the upstream value is actually an Integer and you cast to String, you get a ClassCastException at runtime. Fix that, and a subtle typo bites next: the JSON declares an input variable movieId but the worker reads inputData.get(movieid), which returns null and you get a NullPointerException downstream. None of this is visible until the workflow runs. public class GetMovieWorker implements Worker { @Override public TaskResult execute(Task task) { Map<String, Object> inputData = task.getInputData(); long movieId = (Integer) inputData.get("movieId"); // cast, fingers crossed // more logic here } } Verbosity. Defining a couple of tasks is already wordy. A real workflow’s JSON balloons into hundreds of lines that are difficult to review or refactor. A complex branching workflow becomes a single large JSON blob that no one wants to touch. { "name": "wrap_movie_workflow", "version": 1, "semver": "0.0.1", "schemaVersion": 2, "restartable": true, "workflowStatusListenerEnabled": false, "ownerEmail": "team@netflix.com", "timeoutPolicy": "ALERT_ONLY", "timeoutSeconds": 0, "tasks": [ { "name": "get_movie", "taskReferenceName": "movie", "type": "SIMPLE", "inputParameters": { "movieId": "${workflow.input.movieId}" } }, { "name": "wrap_movie", "taskReferenceName": "wrapMovie", "type": "SIMPLE", "inputParameters": { "movie": "${movie.output}" } } ] } How the Java DSL works @TaskMethod public Movie getMovie(long movieId) { /* real worker logic */ } @TaskMethod public WrappedMovie wrapMovie(Movie movie) { /* real worker logic */ } @WorkflowStub(taskNames = {"movieapp.getMovie", "movieapp.wrapMovie"}) public interface MovieWorkflows { @WorkflowGenerated(name = "movieapp.getMovie") Movie getMovie(int movieId); @WorkflowGenerated(name = "movieapp.wrapMovie") WrappedMovie wrapMovie(Movie movie); @WorkflowMethod(name = "wrap_movie_workflow", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com") default WrappedMovie wrapMovieWorkflow(MovieInput input) { Movie movie = getMovie(input.getMovieId()); // long in, Movie out (checked) return wrapMovie(movie); // Movie in, WrappedMovie out (checked) } } The DSL has two core building blocks. The first, @TaskMethod, is a method that is executed at runtime and can contain arbitrary code. Crucially, it takes and returns real types: a getMovie task can take a long movieId and return a Movie object directly, with no maps and no casts. The second, @WorkflowMethod, is a method that is not executed and cannot contain arbitrary code. It expresses the workflow as ordinary method calls (call getMovie(…), then pass the result to wrapMovie(…)), and a Gradle build plugin parses it into a Conductor JSON definition at build time. The server does not see the Java code. It gets the same JSON it always has. Code generation is central to how this works. In the @WorkflowStub annotation you declare the task and workflow names you want to use, and at build time the Gradle plugin generates their input and output types along with typed stub methods that you call inside a @WorkflowMethod. Those generated stubs are what let the method body compile against real signatures with full type safety. Because the stubs are generated from names rather than shared code, teams can reuse each other’s tasks and workflows without sharing libraries. Real control flow, expressed in Java The examples above are linear, but most production workflows branch, loop, and fan out. The DSL expresses these as the Java constructs you’d reach for anyway, and the SDK parses them into the corresponding Conductor operators. A useful mental model: you’re describing a workflow graph in Java, not running Java, so the parser only supports the constructs that map cleanly to Conductor (if/else, switch, do-while, parallel forks, sub-workflow calls) and asks you to express a few things its way. Iteration, for instance, is always a do-while, since there are no for or while tasks in Conductor. A common shape is to kick off work, poll until it settles, then branch on the outcome, which is a do-while loop wrapped around an if/else: @WorkflowMethod(name = "process_asset_workflow", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com") default void processAssetWorkflow(AssetInput input) { JobStatus status = submitJob(input); do { // loops are do-while status = checkStatus(input.getJobId()); } while (status.getState() == "PENDING"); if (status.getState() == "SUCCEEDED") { // branch on the result publish(input); } else { flagForReview(input); } } Independent work runs concurrently with ParallelExecution.fork(…) plus allOf(…) (a FORK and JOIN), and any other @WorkflowMethod can be called as a sub-workflow just by listing it in workflowNames: @WorkflowStub( taskNames = {"movieapp.getMovie", "movieapp.enrichMovie", "movieapp.getArtwork", "movieapp.refreshCache", "movieapp.publishPage"}, workflowNames = {"movieapp.localize_page_workflow"}) public interface MoviePageWorkflows { // stubs not shown for brevity @WorkflowMethod(name = "prepare_movie_page", ownerEmail = "team@netflix.com") default void prepareMoviePage(MoviePageInput input) { // three independent branches, run in parallel Fork<WrappedMovie> details = ParallelExecution.fork(() -> { Movie movie = getMovie(input.getMovieId()); return enrichMovie(movie); }); Fork<Artwork> art = ParallelExecution.fork(() -> getArtwork(input.getMovieId())); Fork<Void> cache = ParallelExecution.fork(this::refreshCache); ParallelExecution.allOf(details, art, cache); // FORK_JOIN and JOIN WrappedMovie enriched = details.get(); Artwork artwork = art.get(); LocalizedPage localized = localizePageWorkflow(input); // sub-workflow call publishPage(enriched, artwork, localized); } } Sharing tasks and workflows across applications Teams shouldn’t re-implement common tasks. Listing another team’s task or workflow in your @WorkflowStub is enough to call it like a local method, or invoke it as a sub-workflow, and the shared POJO types (a Movie, say) come along directly, with no copy-pasting between codebases. Feature parity and rapid adoption The SDK is gaining rapid adoption and has become the primary choice for authoring new workflows at Netflix. We continue to invest in the developer experience, with intelligent IDE plugins, better debugging, and an integrated testing framework so that testing a workflow in code feels like testing any other code. In production: Netflix Ads Netflix Ads runs complex, multi-step processes on Conductor with the Workflow SDK, and three examples show the range. Creative ingestion is a heavily branching pipeline where the SDK turned a sprawling JSON blob into type-safe, testable code, and a sequential run strategy eliminated a duplicate-processing race by serializing work per creative. Advertiser certificate management automates a previously manual, hard-to-scale process across several system integrations, with downstream automation when certificates expire. And Data Clean Rooms are privacy-preserving environments where Netflix and a partner run joint analysis on shared data, built on the SDK from day one. Provisioning a clean room is a multi-day sequence (create at a vendor, wait for the partner to join, activate, and eventually archive) that previously relied on hand-rolled async polling. Re-authored as Conductor workflows, each phase became a durable, observable state machine with automatic retries, state that survives restarts, and long partner waits that yield rather than hold a thread. The common thread is that the SDK made multi-process, multi-integration workflows easy to author and maintain, and let teams lean on Conductor’s reliability and visibility instead of hand-rolling retries and distributed locking. What’s next Like the last time we wrote about Conductor, the road ahead is less a fixed roadmap than a wish-list, a sense of where we’re headed, shaped by what teams keep asking for. On scale, the demands keep growing. As Netflix expands into new content types, like live, games, and podcasts, we anticipate our workflow load could grow 5x in the coming year, and the engine work described above is what gives us confidence we can absorb it without re-architecting again. On developer experience, the Workflow SDK now covers all task types, so the focus shifts to the experience around writing workflows: a richer integrated testing story so a workflow can be validated against real worker behavior as easily as any other code, deeper agent tooling such as skills, plugins, and MCPs, and safe schema evolution: a schema registry for shared tasks and workflows, with guardrails that block non-backward-compatible changes so they can evolve without breaking the teams that depend on it. On execution control, sequential is only the first run strategy. A family of richer policies is on the roadmap, including running N at a time per key, idempotent de-duplication, keep-first and keep-latest, and combinations of these, to cover the coordination patterns teams currently hand-build. And managed tasks will keep expanding the ways Conductor can run compute directly, beyond today’s container and serverless function integrations. None of this is exhaustive, and priorities shift with the workloads we take on. But the direction is consistent: keep the overhead low, keep authoring safe and simple, and keep widening the range of work a single workflow can reliably coordinate. Acknowledgments Netflix Conductor is built and operated by the Enterprise Workflow Platform team, with contributions from many partner teams across the company. Andrew Seier, Anoop Panicker, Christian Johnson, Christine Yu, Jasmine Lee, Jiaofen Xu, Michael Torku, Peter Lau, Prashant Rastogi, Ryan Kastilani Surafel Korse and Victor Lee have contributed to Conductor. We thank Charles Zhao, Sumukh Shivaprakash and the teams in the Content and Business Products and Ads organizations for their guidance and constructive feedback while developing and operating Conductor. items.title: Behind the Scenes: Evolving Netflix’s Ads Event Pipeline for Live — Part II
items.author: Netflix Technology Blog
items.content: By Yogesh Nagarur Introduction In Part 1 of this series, we shared how Netflix built the Ads Event pipeline and approached it as a system design problem: replacing fragmented pipelines with a centralized collection, enrichment, and a standard data contract. The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII. If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it. Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime. Let’s dive in. A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata Registry When an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. The client device, by contrast, knows almost nothing: just an opaque token and when to send each event. Enrichment is the act of reuniting the two. In the architecture from Part 1, that reunion happened through the Ads Metadata Registry, a Key-Value store: When the ad server made a decision, it wrote the metadata for that impression into the registry. It encoded only reference identifiers into the opaque token returned to the device, keeping the token small. Later, when the client fired an event carrying that token, the Ads Event Publisher decoded the token, looked up the metadata in the registry, and stitched the two together into an enriched ad event. This design served us well. The registry was globally replicated, which gave us a useful property almost for free: an event arriving in any region could find its metadata regardless of where the ad was decided. It future-proofed the token against ever-growing metadata, and it carried us through the first phase of Netflix’s advertising growth. The ad server writes per-impression metadata to the globally replicated registry on the serving path, and the Ads Event Publisher reads it back to enrich each client event. But as we looked ahead, especially to ads on live streams, the limits of this design became clear. Why we needed to evolve The forcing function was Live. Netflix’s live slate has grown rapidly, from NFL games to blockbuster fight nights to the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2027, and viewership keeps growing. That traffic looks nothing like Subscription Video on Demand (SVOD): a single event can surge toward tens of millions of concurrent viewers within minutes, then drain just as fast when it ends. Building the ad pipeline for Live meant building for that trajectory. To see why the old design could not get there, let’s put some numbers on it. When Netflix streamed the Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson fight to more than 100 million viewers, a single ad break at that scale would generate an enormous volume of ad events. Serving those ads in the old design would have meant writing metadata for each of them to the Metadata Registry and waiting for acknowledgment before the ads could serve: millions of must-succeed database writes per second on the ad-serving critical path. That pattern created three core problems at Live scale: It was a scaling bottleneck. Every ad and every ad break is a write. Multiply that by tens of millions of concurrent viewers, keep it non-lossy (a dropped write is a dropped ad, and lost revenue), add Live’s spiky on/off pattern, and the write load becomes enormous. But you cannot safely scale the registry up once the event starts. Adding nodes reshuffles data across the cluster to rebalance it, and doing that in the middle of a live event could slow or even fail the very writes you are adding capacity for. That leaves one safe option: pre-scaling for the peak in advance and hoping the forecast is accurate. Fewer dependencies on the critical path. Serving an ad meant a synchronous, must-succeed write to the registry, followed by a wait for its acknowledgment. Every system on the critical path is one more thing that can stop an ad from serving, and the metadata registry had no fallback, so an unhealthy registry meant serving stopped. Taking hard dependencies off that path was the goal, and the registry was the biggest one we could remove. It put event freshness at risk. If writing slowed down under load, or lookups timed out, events spilled into retries and dead-letter queues, and enriched ad events were delivered late. Some systems might be fine, but others, such as frequency capping, cannot. It needs events under a strict SLA to decide whether the next selected ad can run without breaking policies. So we asked a simple question: the ad server already knows and logs everything about the ad it served. Does it really need to write that to a database on the hot path? Can we match that against the downstream Kafka stream of client events, which is always there, after the fact? The write leaves the critical path entirely; no shared datastore outage can stop serving, and enrichment becomes something we scale elastically with Live rather than a cluster we babysit. Matching two streams after the fact is a streaming join, and that is where Flink comes in. Why Flink We chose Apache Flink because near-real-time, stateful stream processing is exactly what it is built for, and because it has deep, production-tested platform support at Netflix. Just as important, we already knew how to run it. As Part 1 noted, our Ads Sessionizer is a large stateful Flink job, so operating one at scale, tuning state, checkpoints, and recovery under production load, was familiar ground for the team. Enrichment on Flink was built on that experience rather than starting from scratch. The new architecture At its core, the new Ads Event Publisher is built as an Apache Flink streaming job. Each event moves through a handful of stages: Normalize. Client events arrive from several sources, including SVOD, live, playback, and embedded ad breaks, each with a slightly different shape. We first normalize them into a common form. Re-route. Client events and response events may appear in different regions; we inspect and reroute them to the correct job-processing region for a successful join. Join. The heart of the job: we match each client event to the ad-serving response for the same impression, enriching it with the full serving context using a KeyedCoProcessFunction Deduplicate. Revenue-bearing events are de-duplicated, so nothing is counted twice. Publish. We extract measurement beacons for our partners and route the enriched ad event to its downstream consumers. The ad server logs responses to Kafka rather than writing to a registry; the Flink job joins responses with client events in real time and routes enriched ad events downstream. The join is the interesting part. Client events and ad serving responses arrive on separate streams at different times, so the job holds recent responses in memory and matches events against them over a 60-minute window. Three things can happen: The response is already there when an event arrives → we enrich it on the spot. The event arrives first → we hold it for a configuration duration (currently set to 60 minutes) until the matching response shows up, then enrich it. No response arrives within the window → we mark the event as unmatched for later recovery. We built the join as a custom Flink operator (a KeyedCoProcessFunction) rather than a built-in windowed join. We do not need a windowed join ordering and time-window semantics, since downstream consumers handle ordering; we simply match each client event to its response by key. Owning the operator at its lowest API form lets us control the matching state directly, including how long we hold it and what we do with an event that never matches. This allows us to tune retention per stream or persist unmatched events to a durable store later without rewriting the join. Our goal is always to build a strong base to reap the benefits later as we scale. To make that concrete, picture a member watching a live game. When the ad server decides which ad to show, it logs its response, and a few seconds later, the member’s device fires a “first quartile” event carrying the opaque token. Both arrive at the job keyed to the same impression, and because the response is already waiting, the event is enriched on the spot with its campaign, creative, price, and tracking URLs, then published downstream in near real-time. Why 60 minutes? Almost all events, roughly 99.999% of them, reach the job well before that, so extending the window further would only grow the state store and lengthen checkpoints for a vanishingly small gain. The remaining 0.001% still matters for precise billing and reporting, and we recover those events via a separate path described later on. Cross-region: matching events where their data lives The Metadata Registry handled cross-region enrichment for us because it was built on a globally replicated key-value store: a client event could land in any region and still find its ad’s metadata. Global replication was a feature the platform provided (see Netflix’s Key-Value Data Abstraction Layer), so serving an ad in one region and enriching its events in another was simply not something we had to think about. A streaming join does not come with that convenience, and here the two sides of the join live in different places. The ad serving response stays in the region where the ad was served. The client event, though, is fired by the device, and the device can be anywhere: a member might start an ad on home wifi and switch to mobile data partway through, and that network change can route the event to a different region than the one that served the ad. So a client event is routed to a region that does not have the matching serving response. The tempting fix is to stream every region’s serving responses into every other region so that each region can match any client event locally. We rejected it: that would mean every region storing every serving response worldwide, the vast majority of which will never be used in the join, which is wasteful in both cost and compute. Instead, we treat this as a routing problem and route the client event rather than replicating the response. We encode the serving region into the ad token, so when a client event arrives in the wrong region, we forward it to the region that owns its response. For example, an ad is served in us-east-2, the member’s device switches from wifi to mobile data mid-ad, and the resulting event arrives in us-east-1. That region reads the token, sees the ad belongs to eu-west-1, and forwards the event back there, where its serving response is waiting. Only the small trickle of genuinely cross-region events pays for the extra hop. Catching the long tail of late-arriving events Sixty minutes covers the vast majority of events, but not all of them. A device may have been offline, an ad paused, or an engagement event delayed by hours. Rather than drop these stragglers, we set them aside and recover them through a companion path: an hourly Spark batch job, orchestrated by Maestro, Netflix’s workflow orchestrator, re-pairs each straggler with its serving response from our data warehouse (which has a far longer retention than our in-stream window) and publishes it through the same downstream sinks. This keeps the streaming job’s memory bounded while still catching the long tail.
